title: OMANAKUTTAN versus THE STATE OF KERALA
case_title: Omanakuttan v. The State of Kerala
aggravating_circumstances: Use of acid, extensive injuries, long hospitalisation
mitigating_circumstances: Accused is 63 years old, offence committed in 1997
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.326 IPC, sentenced to simple imprisonment for one year and fine of Rs. 5,000/-
offence_finally_established: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt by use of acid
neutral_facts: The accused and the victim were neighbors. The accused poured acid on the victim's left side while the victim was walking on a road. The victim sustained extensive acid burns on his forehead, scalp, neck, back of the chest, left buttock, and front of the left thigh. The victim was hospitalized for over 50 days and was unable to perform daily routines during this period. The victim's mother and other witnesses corroborated the incident. The treating doctor confirmed the acid burns and noted the potential for disfigurement. 5,000/-.
offence_severity: imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine
physical_harm: extensive acid burns involving forehead, scalp, neck, back of chest, left buttock and front of left thigh
number_of_offences: One offence was charged and upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The fact that the appellant poured acid on the body of the victim was proved beyond any doubt by the evidence on record, including the testimony of the victim PW-1 as also his mother PW-2. The fact that the victim sustained extensive acid burns on the left side of his body also stood duly proved in his testimony read with the testimony of the doctor PW-8.
witness_credibility: The court thoroughly examined the material on record and returned concurrent findings against the appellant. The testimony of the victim PW-1 and his mother PW-2 was corroborated, and the doctor PW-8's testimony was considered in context with the victim's own account.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 26.11.1997; Trial judgment: 04.12.2002; High Court decision: 23.09.2004; Supreme Court decision: 05.06.2018
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: Thomas P. Joseph, Sr. Adv., K. Parameshwar, Ms. Rajitha T. H., Ms. Benny Antony; Counsel for the State: Nishe Rajen Shonker, Anu K. Joy, Alim Anvar, Reegan S. Bel
investigation_status: Charge sheet filed under Section 326 read with Section 34 IPC; trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction under Section 326 IPC; High Court: Affirmed conviction; Supreme Court: Dismissed appeal
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellant poured acid on the victim due to previous enmity, causing extensive acid burns involving the forehead, scalp, neck, back of chest, left buttock, and front of left thigh. The victim was hospitalized for 50 days, and the trial court convicted the appellant under Section 326 IPC.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the victim did not state he was in severe bodily pain for 20 days or that he suffered disfigurement, and the doctor testified that the victim could carry out daily routines during hospitalization, suggesting the case did not meet the criteria for grievous hurt under Section 320 IPC.
legal_principle_applied: The court applied the legal principle that grievous hurt under Section 320 IPC includes severe bodily pain for twenty days or inability to follow ordinary pursuits, and that acid, being a corrosive substance, qualifies as a dangerous means under Section 326 IPC.
precedent_relied_upon: Not stated
sentencing_rationale: The sentence was deemed inadequate given the gravity of the offence, but the court refrained from enhancing it due to the appellant's age and the offence's occurrence in 1997.
judicial_mitigating_factors: The court considered the appellant's age and the fact that the offence was committed in 1997 as mitigating factors.
neutral_facts_raw: The accused and the victim were neighbors. The accused poured acid on the victim's left side while the victim was walking on a road. The victim sustained extensive acid burns on his forehead, scalp, neck, back of the chest, left buttock, and front of the left thigh. The victim was hospitalized for over 50 days and was unable to perform daily routines during this period. The victim's mother and other witnesses corroborated the incident. The treating doctor confirmed the acid burns and noted the potential for disfigurement. The accused was found guilty of causing grievous hurt by dangerous means, specifically acid, and was sentenced to simple imprisonment for one year and a fine of Rs. 5,000/-.

title: MANGESH versus STATE OF MAHARASHTRA
case_title: A MANG ESH v. STATE OF MAHARASHTRA
mitigating_circumstances: Loss of self control, heat of passion, lack of premeditation, no undue advantage or cruel manner
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under Section 302 IPC
offence_finally_established: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder
neutral_facts: The accused had a conflict with the victim due to the victim's relationship with the accused's sister. On the night of the incident, the accused saw the victim and his sister together and assaulted the victim with a knife. The victim was taken to the hospital, where he made two dying declarations stating that the accused had caused knife injuries to him. The victim later died from the injuries. The medical report indicated that the injuries were not inflicted with full force, and the accused did not cause fatal injuries with the knife. The accused fled the scene after the assault.
offence_severity: Minimum: 10 years rigorous imprisonment, Maximum: Life imprisonment
physical_harm: Deceased suffered stab injuries, including a fatal stab wound to the chest and non-fatal injuries to the thigh and other parts of the body
number_of_offences: Charged under Section 302 IPC; finally upheld under Section 304 Part-I IPC
premeditation_planning: The court found no premeditation or planning
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the medical evidence indicating that the accused did not stab the deceased with full force, and that the injuries were not fatal in nature, with the fatal injury being 'cavity deep' and not more severe.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the credibility of the main witnesses, including the sister of the accused, as hostile to the prosecution's case, but found that the dying declarations were not contradictory and could form the basis of the conviction.
trial_duration: {'dates_of_offence': '30.4.2003', 'trial_judgment': '16.3.2004', 'high_court_decision': '25.8.2009', 'supreme_court_decision': 'B January 05, 2011'}
legal_representation: {'accused': 'Gaurav Agarwal', 'state': 'Shabkar Chillarge, Sanjay V. Kharde and Asha Gopalan Nair'}
investigation_status: Charge sheet filed
appeal_history: {'trial_court': 'Convicted under Section 302 IPC', 'high_court': 'Affirmed the conviction under Section 302 IPC', 'supreme_court': 'Altered conviction from Section 302 IPC to Section 304 Part-I IPC and awarded ten years rigorous imprisonment'}
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the accused's sister had a love affair with the deceased, which the accused did not like, leading to altercations. On the fateful night, the accused assaulted the deceased with a knife, resulting in his death. The deceased made dying declarations implicating the accused in the attack.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the accused's actions were not pre-meditated and were a result of sudden provocation. The accused did not intend to cause death, as evidenced by the nature of the injuries inflicted and the fact that he fled the scene.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that the intention to cause death can be inferred from various circumstances, including the nature of the weapon, the force used, and the context of the incident. The court emphasized that each case must be considered on its own facts.
precedent_relied_upon: Pulicherla Nagaraju alias Nagaraja Reddy v. State of A.P. AIR 2006 SC 3010; Kai/ash v. State of M.P. (2006 (11) SCC 420; Karuppusamy & Anr. v. State of Tamil Nadu (2006) 11 SCC 459; Sridhar Bhuyan v. State of Orissa AIR 2004 SC 4100; Gali Venkataiah v. State of Andhra Pradesh AIR 2008 SC 462
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed to meet the ends of justice, as the act was not pre-meditated and the accused did not act in a cruel or unusual manner. The court found that the conviction should be altered from Section 302 to Section 304 Part-I IPC.
judicial_mitigating_factors: The court considered that the accused acted in the heat of passion, did not take undue advantage, and did not act in a cruel or unusual manner.

On the night of the incident, the accused saw the victim and his sister together and assaulted the victim with a knife. The victim was taken to the hospital, where he made two dying declarations stating that the accused had caused knife injuries to him. The victim later died from the injuries. The medical report indicated that the injuries were not inflicted with full force, and the accused did not cause fatal injuries with the knife. The accused fled the scene after the assault.

title: DHARAM DEO YADAV versus STATE OF U.P.
case_title: DHARAM DEO YADAV v. STATE OF U.P.
confession: Admission made by accused, relied on
aggravating_circumstances: Strangulation of a young girl from a foreign country
mitigating_circumstances: No previous criminal record, poor socioeconomic status
trial_court_outcome: Convicted and sentenced to death
neutral_facts: The accused, a tourist guide, was last seen with the deceased, a 22-year-old foreign woman, at a railway station. The deceased was later found missing, and her body was discovered buried in the accused's house. The accused confessed to the crime and led authorities to the body. A DNA test confirmed the deceased's identity, and the prosecution established a chain of circumstantial evidence linking the accused to the crime. The accused had no prior criminal record and was from a poor background.
offence_severity: Minimum/Maximum: 302 IPC (life imprisonment or death sentence)
physical_harm: Strangulation leading to death
number_of_offences: Multiple counts charged, but only some were finally upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the DNA test results showing the skeleton recovered from the accused's house was that of the deceased, Diana, and that the accused had strangulated her to death. The court also relied on the circumstantial evidence, including the last seen theory and the accused's confession under Section 313 Cr.P.C.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as credible, noting that their oral evidence, although circumstantial, formed a complete chain of circumstances leading to the conclusion of the accused's guilt. However, the court also pointed out that the witnesses' accounts were not entirely reliable and needed to be corroborated with other evidence.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 10.08.1997; Trial judgment: 30.09.2005; High Court decision: Not stated; Supreme Court decision: Not stated
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: Sunil Kr. Singh, Mukti Singh, Dr. Kailash Chand; Counsel for the State: Ratnakar Dash, M. R. Shamshad, Vikrant Yadav, Shashank Singh
investigation_status: Charge sheet filed (Ex. Ka40 and Ka41); trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction and death sentence; High Court: Confirmed death sentence; Supreme Court: Death sentence commuted to life imprisonment
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the accused was last seen with the deceased, and the DNA test confirmed the identity of the skeleton found in the accused's house as that of the deceased. The prosecution also emphasized that the accused's false answers during the 313 Cr.P.C. statement provided additional links in the chain of circumstances, leading to the conclusion that the accused was guilty beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the case rested solely on circumstantial evidence, which was inconclusive and inconsistent. They also questioned the reliability and admissibility of the DNA report, suggesting that the skeleton could have been planted and that the manner of the crime was not established, thus not qualifying as a rarest of rare case.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that circumstantial evidence can lead to a conviction if the circumstances form a complete and conclusive chain of events, leaving no reasonable doubt about the accused's guilt.
precedent_relied_upon: State of Andhra Pradesh vs. Gangula Satya Murthy (1997) 1 sec 272: 1996 (8) Suppl. SCR 808; A.N. B Venkatesh vs. State of Karnataka (2005) 7 SCC 714; Sandeep vs. State of Uttar Pradesh (2012) 6 sec 107:2012 (5) SCR 952; Daubert vs. Merrell Dow Pharmaceuticals, Inc. 509 U.S. 579 (1993); Anthony D'souza vs. State of Karnataka (2003) 1 SCC 259; Shankar Kisanrao Khade vs. State of Maharashtra (2013) 5 SCC 546
sentencing_rationale: The death sentence was reduced to life imprisonment because the manner in which the crime was committed was not established, and thus the case did not fall under the rarest of rare category.
judicial_mitigating_factors: The accused had no previous criminal records, and the manner of the crime was not established, which mitigated the severity of the sentence.
other_sentence_order: Life imprisonment and 20 years of rigorous imprisonment, over and above the period already undergone by the accused, without any remission.
neutral_facts_raw: The accused, a tourist guide, was last seen with the deceased, a 22-year-old foreign woman, at a railway station. The deceased was later found missing, and her body was discovered buried in the accused's house. The accused confessed to the crime and led authorities to the body. A DNA test confirmed the deceased's identity, and the prosecution established a chain of circumstantial evidence linking the accused to the crime. The accused had no prior criminal record and was from a poor background.

title: MADALA VENKATA NARSIMHA RAO versus STATE OF A.P.
case_title: MADALA VENKATA NARSIMHA RAO v. STATE OF A.P.
aggravating_circumstances: Accused ran away from the scene with blood-stained clothes, victim's dying declaration
trial_court_outcome: Acquitted of all charges
high_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302 and s.376 IPC
neutral_facts: The accused was a laborer working for the victim's family. The victim was alone at home when her brother sent the accused to perform some work. Witnesses saw the accused running out of the house in blood-stained clothes after hearing the victim's cries. The accused pushed the witnesses away as they entered the house. The victim told the witnesses that the accused hit her with a chutney grinder after she slapped him. The victim later died en route to the hospital. A post-mortem report suggested rape, but the doctor who conducted the post-mortem did not testify.
offence_severity: Life imprisonment (Section 302 IPC) and rape (Section 376 IPC)
physical_harm: The victim was hit with a chutney grinder and stabbed with a knife, leading to her death.
number_of_offences: The accused was charged with both murder and rape, but the High Court upheld both charges, and the Supreme Court confirmed the murder conviction but rejected the rape charge.
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the presence of the accused at the scene of the crime, his running away from the house with blood-stained clothes, and the dying declaration of the victim stating that the accused had assaulted her with a chutney grinder. The court also noted the medical opinion of the post-mortem report suggesting rape, but found it insufficient due to the doctor not being examined as a witness.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as credible, noting their consistent testimony about the accused's conduct and the victim's statements. The court found no indication that the witnesses had fabricated their accounts to implicate the accused.
post_offence_conduct: The accused ran away from the scene of the crime with blood-stained clothes and was seen on the street in that condition, which the court considered as conduct indicative of guilt.
trial_duration: {'dates_of_offence': '4th December, 1998', 'trial_judgment': '18th June 2004', 'high_court_decision': '14th February 2008', 'supreme_court_decision': '27th November 2012'}
legal_representation: {'accused': 'Vikas Upadhyay (for B.S. Banthia)', 'state': 'Shishir Pinaki, Suchitra Hranghwal (for D. Mahesh Babu)'}
investigation_status: Challan filed by the police, post-mortem conducted, trial completed
appeal_history: {'trial_court': 'Acquitted the accused', 'high_court': 'Convicted the accused', 'supreme_court': 'Partly allowed the appeal, confirmed conviction for murder'}
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the accused was present at the scene of the crime, ran away from the house in blood-stained clothes, and that the victim's dying declaration implicated him in the murder. The post-mortem report also suggested rape, though the doctor did not testify.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the case was based on circumstantial evidence and that there were numerous discrepancies in the witnesses' testimonies. They contended that the prosecution's case was not sufficiently proven and that the benefit of the doubt should go to the accused.
legal_principle_applied: To secure a conviction on circumstantial evidence, the prosecution must prove its case by cogent, reliable, and admissible evidence. Each relevant circumstance must be proved like any other fact, and upon a composite reading thereof, it must lead to a high degree of probability that it is only the accused who committed the alleged offence.
precedent_relied_upon: Munna Kumar Upadhyay v. State of A.P. (2012) 6 SCC 174; Syed Ahmed v. State of Kamataka (2012) 8 SCC 527
sentencing_rationale: The Supreme Court confirmed the conviction and sentence for murder under Section 302 of the IPC, as the evidence supported the conclusion that the accused committed the murder, but there was no cogent evidence of rape.
neutral_facts_raw: The accused was a laborer working for the victim's family. The victim was alone at home when her brother sent the accused to perform some work. Witnesses saw the accused running out of the house in blood-stained clothes after hearing the victim's cries. The accused pushed the witnesses away as they entered the house. The victim told the witnesses that the accused hit her with a chutney grinder after she slapped him. The victim later died en route to the hospital. A post-mortem report suggested rape, but the doctor who conducted the post-mortem did not testify. The trial court acquitted the accused, while the high court convicted him of murder and rape. The Supreme Court upheld the conviction for murder but found no evidence of rape.

title: MANIK & ORS. versus THE STATE OF MAHARASHTRA
case_title: Manik & Ors. v. The State of Maharashtra
aggravating_circumstances: Custodial torture, concocted case, false evidence, disappearance of body
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.304-II r/w s.34, s.330, s.348, s.387 r/w s.34, and other charges
high_court_outcome: Confirmed conviction and sentences except under s.201 r/w s.34
offence_finally_established: Custodial torture under s.330, s.348, s.387 r/w s.34
neutral_facts: The accused, who were members of the police force, were alleged to have subjected the victim to custodial torture and tampered with evidence. The victim was taken into police custody for interrogation in connection with a house-breaking incident. During interrogation, the victim was subjected to third-degree methods, resulting in his death. An unidentified body, which was burnt and buried, was found in a forest area. The prosecution alleged that the accused concocted a case to escape prosecution for the custodial death by making a person named Dipak Lokhande impersonate the victim and stage an escape.
offence_severity: Minimum 3 months rigorous imprisonment / Maximum 7 years rigorous imprisonment
physical_harm: Injuries and death caused by custodial torture
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the evidence of custodial torture and the testimonies of witnesses such as PW-1, PW-3, PW-4, PW-16, PW-20, PW-21, PW-22, and others, which established that the deceased was in the custody of the appellants and subjected to torture.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the credibility of the witnesses with caution, noting that some witnesses, like PW-3, were hostile and their testimonies were not fully reliable. However, their statements were corroborated by other witnesses, and the court relied on the overall consistency of the testimonies to establish the custodial torture.
custody_duration: Shama was in police custody from 16.12.1995 at least, and suffered prolonged third-degree treatment till 24.12.1995
trial_duration: Offence: 07.12.1995; Trial judgment: 12.07.2011; High Court decision: 12.07.2011; Supreme Court decision: 25 September 2024
legal_representation: S. Nagamuthu, Sr. Adv., Shivaji M. Jadhav, Ms. Apurva, Brij Kishor Sah, Adarsh Kumar Pandey, Vighesh Singh, Advs. for the Appellants; Shrirang B. Varma, Siddharth Dharmadhikari, Aaditya Aniruddha Pandey, Bharat Bagla, Sourav Singh, Aditya Krishna, Advs. for the Respondent
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: {'trial_court': 'Conviction and sentences confirmed except under Section 201 r/w. s.34, IPC', 'high_court': 'Conviction and sentences confirmed except under Section 201 r/w. s.34, IPC', 'supreme_court': 'Criminal Appeal No.1614/2012 stood abated; A2, A3, A4, A5 convicted under s.330, 348 and 387 r/w. s.34, IPC; others acquitted of other offences'}
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellants-convicts committed the heinous crime of custodial torture leading to the death of victim-S, and concocted a case to escape prosecution for custodial death by making Dipak Lokhande impersonate the victim and stage an escape.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the dead body found in the forest was not identified as that of victim-S, and that the prosecution's case was based on fabricated evidence. They also contended that the appellants were entitled to acquittal due to the lack of evidence regarding the homicidal death of victim-S.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that when sufficient evidence is available to conclude that a victim died due to custodial torture, the police personnel who caused the death must also be held responsible for the disappearance of the body.
precedent_relied_upon: Central Bureau of Investigation v. Kishore Singh, Noor Aga v. State of Punjab and Anr., V. Venkata Subbarao v. State, Vishnu Dutt Sharma v. Daya Sapra, Bhagwan Singh and Another v. State of Punjab, Sevaka Perumal & Anr. v. State of Tamil Nadu
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed based on the conviction for custodial torture under Sections 330, 348, and 387 read with Section 34, IPC, as the court found the appellants guilty of causing the victim's death through torture while in their custody.
judicial_aggravating_factors: The court considered the aggravating factor of the appellants' role in causing the victim's death through custodial torture and their attempt to fabricate evidence to evade justice.
neutral_facts_raw: The accused, who were members of the police force, were alleged to have subjected the victim to custodial torture and tampered with evidence. The victim was taken into police custody for interrogation in connection with a house-breaking incident. During interrogation, the victim was subjected to third-degree methods, resulting in his death. An unidentified body, which was burnt and buried, was found in a forest area. The prosecution alleged that the accused concocted a case to escape prosecution for the custodial death by making a person named Dipak Lokhande impersonate the victim and stage an escape. The trial court found that the prosecution succeeded in establishing the charge under s.304-II r/w s.34 against some accused, while others were found guilty under other charges. The high court confirmed the conviction and sentences except for certain charges.

title: MANI versus STATE OF KERALA AND OTHERS
case_title: Mani v. State of Kerala and Others
statutory_provisions: IPC s. 300, Exception 4, s. 304 (Part I); s. 34 IPC
trial_court_outcome: Convicted accused Nos. 1 to 4 u/ss. 302, 341 and 324 r/w s. 34 IPC
high_court_outcome: Upheld conviction of accused No. 1 u/s. 302, and conviction of accused Nos. 2 to 4 u/ss. 324 and 341 r/w s. 34
neutral_facts: The incident occurred when eight individuals, who were celebrating their party's victory in panchayat elections, decided to go towards Chozhiyamkod. The accused, riding on two motorcycles, suddenly confronted the group. The accused had no prior knowledge that the victims were moving towards Chozhiyamkod. A fight ensued, resulting in injuries to the victims. The deceased, Soman, was stabbed on the chest by the accused, leading to his death. The injuries inflicted on the accused were not serious, and the accused had no prior enmity with the victims. The prosecution's case relied on the testimony of injured witnesses, but the statements were inconsistent.
offence_severity: Minimum: 10 years, Maximum: Life imprisonment (Section 304 Part I)
physical_harm: Death of one person and injuries to eight persons
number_of_offences: Seven offences charged, three finally upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The court accepted the testimony of the injured witnesses that the appellant stabbed the deceased, but found inconsistencies in their accounts of the injuries caused and the genesis of the dispute.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as inconsistent in their accounts of the injuries caused, but noted that they consistently deposed that the appellant caused the death of the deceased.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 28.09.2005; Trial judgment: 24.11.2011; High Court decision: 02.02.2016; Supreme Court decision: APRIL 01, 2019
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: Not stated; Counsel for the State: Not stated
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction of accused Nos. 1 to 4; High Court: Upheld conviction of accused No. 1 and conviction of accused Nos. 2 to 4; Supreme Court: Partly allowed appeal of the accused and dismissed the appeal of the State
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the accused had a common intention to cause death and that the victims were attacked with weapons, leading to the death of Soman. They also claimed that the accused were part of a group creating trouble at the place of occurrence.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the appellant had acted in self-defence as he had received injuries, and that the incident was a sudden fight without premeditation, thus not amounting to murder. They also contended that there was no common intention to cause death.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that culpable homicide not amounting to murder falls under Exception 4 of Section 300 IPC, which covers cases of sudden fight without premeditation and in heat of passion.
precedent_relied_upon: Dharam Pal and Others v. State of Haryana AIR 1978 SC 1492; Nand Kishore v. State of Madhya Pradesh AIR 2011 SC 2775
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed considering the appellant had already undergone more than seven years of actual imprisonment, and the circumstances of the occurrence, with the sentence being modified to the period already served while maintaining a fine of Rs. 20,000.
judicial_mitigating_factors: The court considered the sudden fight without premeditation, the appellant's injury, and the fact that the death occurred in heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel.
neutral_facts_raw: The incident occurred when eight individuals, who were celebrating their party's victory in panchayat elections, decided to go towards Chozhiyamkod. The accused, riding on two motorcycles, suddenly confronted the group. The accused had no prior knowledge that the victims were moving towards Chozhiyamkod. A fight ensued, resulting in injuries to the victims. The deceased, Soman, was stabbed on the chest by the accused, leading to his death. The injuries inflicted on the accused were not serious, and the accused had no prior enmity with the victims. The prosecution's case relied on the testimony of injured witnesses, but the statements were inconsistent. The accused consistently claimed that the deceased was killed by the appellant.

title: ABDUL NAWAZ versus STATE OF WEST BENGAL
case_title: ABDUL NAWAZ v. STATE OF WEST BENGAL
trial_court_outcome: Convicted u/s 302 IPC and sentenced to imprisonment for life
high_court_outcome: Upheld conviction and sentence of life imprisonment
offence_finally_established: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder punishable u/s 304(1) of the IPC
neutral_facts: The accused and his companions were involved in a scuffle with a deceased Head Constable while attempting to recover a dinghy. The accused picked up a dao, inflicted a blow on the deceased's head, and pushed him into the sea. The deceased's body was later recovered from the sea. The prosecution case was based on the testimony of witnesses who described the sequence of events, including the use of a dao and the pushing of the deceased into the sea.
physical_harm: Head injury and bleeding, pushed into the sea leading to drowning
number_of_offences: Multiple offences charged, but only the appellant's conviction under Section 302 was upheld initially; later, he was convicted under Section 304 (Part I)
premeditation_planning: Not found; the act was committed in a sudden fight without pre-meditation
motive: Not identified; the motive was to recover the dinghy
key_evidence_accepted: The return of the appellant to recover the second dinghy, a scuffle taking place between the appellant and the deceased Head Constable on board the second dinghy, and the deceased being hit with a 'dao' by the appellant and being pushed into the sea was proved by the evidence on record.
witness_credibility: The depositions of PWs1 and 2 to the extent they proved the above facts were cogent and consistent hence acceptable.
trial_duration: Offence: 19.3.2008; Trial judgment: 30.08.2010; High Court decision: Not stated; Supreme Court decision: 10.5.2012
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: Jaspal Singh, Rauf Rahim, Y. Bansal; Counsel for the State: Ashok Bhan, Asha G. Nair, Sadhna Sandhu, CK Sharma, D.S. Mahra
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction u/s 302 IPC; High Court: Allowed appeals of A-1 to A-3, dismissed appeal of appellant; Supreme Court: Partly allowed the appeal, set aside conviction u/s 302 IPC, convicted u/s 304 (Part-I) and sentenced to 8 years RI
prosecution_argument: The prosecution case was that the appellant and his companions had returned to the place of occurrence only to recover the second dinghy which they had left behind while they had escaped from the spot in the other dinghy. The deceased was assaulted with a 'dao' and pushed into the sea, leading to his death.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the prosecution case was primarily based on the evidence of PWs 1 and 2, which was not worthy of credit. There was no evidence to prove that the injury inflicted by the appellant was in the ordinary course of nature sufficient to cause death. The case fell under Exception 4 to s. 300 IPC due to a sudden fight.
legal_principle_applied: The court applied the legal principle that pushing a person into the sea with a bleeding head injury may not have been with the intention to kill, but it would certainly show the intention of causing a bodily injury as was likely to cause death, within the meaning of s. 300 and s. 304 (Part I) of the IPC.
precedent_relied_upon: Bharwada Bhoginbhai Hirjibhai v. State of Gujarat, 1983 (3) SCR 280; Chinnathaman v. State 2007 (14) SCC 690; Muthu v. State 2007 (11) SCR 911; Arumugam v. State 2008 (14) SCR 309; Ajit Singh v. State of Punjab 2011 (12) SCR 375; Elavarasan v. State 2011 (10) SCR 1147
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the act of the appellant, although resulting in the death of the deceased, was committed without pre-meditation and in the course of a sudden fight, thus falling under s. 304 (Part I) instead of s. 302.
neutral_facts_raw: The accused and his companions were involved in a scuffle with a deceased Head Constable while attempting to recover a dinghy. The accused picked up a dao, inflicted a blow on the deceased's head, and pushed him into the sea. The deceased's body was later recovered from the sea. The prosecution case was based on the testimony of witnesses who described the sequence of events, including the use of a dao and the pushing of the deceased into the sea. The trial court convicted the accused of murder, but the High Court and the Supreme Court re-evaluated the evidence and found that the act of pushing the deceased into the sea, combined with the head injury, constituted culpable homicide not amounting to murder. The Supreme Court upheld the conviction under Section 304(1) of the IPC and sentenced the accused to eight years of imprisonment.

title: ROY FERNANDES versus STATE OF GOA AND ORS.
case_title: Roy Fernandes v. State of Goa and Ors.
trial_court_outcome: Convicted of offences punishable under Sections 143, 148, 323, 325 and 302 read with Section 149
high_court_outcome: Upheld conviction of appellant and accused no.2, set aside conviction of other three
neutral_facts: The accused, a man in his 60s, was involved in a dispute with the victim, a man also in his 60s, over the use of a path near the victim's house. The victim and his companions were attempting to put up a fence around a chapel property when the victim's daughter raised an objection. A van arrived carrying five individuals, including the accused, who intervened. The accused pushed and slapped the victim, causing him to fall. Another accused, who was carrying a knife, stabbed the victim in the thigh, leading to his death. The prosecution alleged that the accused had a common object of preventing the fence from being put up, but the court found no evidence of this.
offence_severity: Minimum: 6 months' imprisonment, Maximum: Life imprisonment and fine of Rs.2,000/-
physical_harm: Deceased suffered profuse bleeding from a stab wound to the thigh, leading to his death
number_of_offences: Five offences/counts charged; four were finally upheld
premeditation_planning: The court found no premeditation or planning
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted that the appellant was unarmed and that the accused no.2 used a knife to stab the deceased, leading to his death. The court also noted that the accused no.2 returned the knife to its cover after the stabbing.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the credibility of the witnesses, noting that PW1 was not a witness to the telephonic conversation between the appellant and 'R', and that the prosecution's case relied on the testimony of PW1 and others, which was scrutinized for its reliability.
post_offence_conduct: The appellant was running a hotel in Goa and earning an amount of Rs. 10-12 lakhs per year, indicating he had the means to pay compensation, but there is no mention of his conduct after the offence in terms of absconding or surrender.
trial_duration: The incident took place on 11th May, 1997. The trial court judgment was dated 22.07.2002. The High Court decision was in the same year, and the Supreme Court judgment was on 1 February 2012.
legal_representation: Sidharth Luthra, Jaiveer Shergil, Rook Ray, Shazia Parveen, Arundhati Katju, Arshdeep Singh, Sanjeeb Panigrahi, Naresh Kumar for the Appellant. A. Subhashini for the Respondents.
investigation_status: Chargesheet filed against the accused persons for offences punishable under Sections 143, 147, 148, 201, 302 and 323 read with Section 149 IPC. The investigation was completed, and the case was committed to the Additional Sessions Judge.
appeal_history: {'trial_court': 'Convicted all the five accused under Sections 143, 148, 323, 325 and 302 read with Section 149 IPC.', 'high_court': 'Upheld the conviction and sentence awarded to the appellant and accused no.2 while setting aside the conviction and sentence awarded to the remaining three accused persons giving them the benefit of doubt.', 'supreme_court': 'Partly allowed the appeal, set aside the conviction and sentence awarded to the appellant under Section 302 read with Section 149 IPC and acquitted the appellant of that charge. Affirmed the conviction for offences punishable under Sections 323 and 325 IPC.'}
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the accused persons had come to the place of occurrence with the common object of killing the deceased, and that the appellant was involved in the act leading to the deceased's death.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the accused persons had come to the spot with a view to overawe and prevent the deceased from putting up the fence, and that the appellant was unarmed and had no knowledge that the accused no.2 was carrying a knife.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that the common object of the unlawful assembly must be established, and that the act of murder must be in prosecution of that common object.
precedent_relied_upon: Khem Karan & Ors. v. The State of U.P. & Anr. 1974 (4) SCC 603; Dharam Pal and Ors. v. State of UP. 1975 (2) SCC 596; Lalji and Ors. v. State of U.P. 1989 (1) SCC 437; Hansa v. State of Punjab 1977 (3) SCC 575; Manish Jalan v. State of Kamataka (2008) 8 SCC 225
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the conviction for offences punishable under Sections 143, 148, 323 and 325 read with Section 149 was justified, and the appellant had already undergone part of the sentence.
judicial_mitigating_factors: The appellant had no criminal antecedents, had suffered trauma from prolonged trial and uncertainty, and was earning a substantial income, making him capable of paying compensation.
other_sentence_order: The appellant was directed to deposit Rs.3,00,000/- towards compensation to the widow of the deceased, Rs.1,00,000/- to PW-6, and Rs.50,000/- to another victim.
neutral_facts_raw: The accused, a man in his 60s, was involved in a dispute with the victim, a man also in his 60s, over the use of a path near the victim's house. The victim and his companions were attempting to put up a fence around a chapel property when the victim's daughter raised an objection. A van arrived carrying five individuals, including the accused, who intervened. The accused pushed and slapped the victim, causing him to fall. Another accused, who was carrying a knife, stabbed the victim in the thigh, leading to his death. The prosecution alleged that the accused had a common object of preventing the fence from being put up, but the court found no evidence of this. The accused was acquitted of murder but convicted of lesser offenses.

title: ANVERSINH @ KIRANSINH FATESINH ZALA versus STATE OF GUJARAT
case_title: Anversinh @ Kiransinh Fatesinh Zala v. State of Gujarat
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under ss.363 and 366 of IPC
neutral_facts: The accused, a young man, was involved in an incident where a minor girl, aged 16, was taken from her parents' custody. The girl was working as a maid and was last seen leaving her workplace with the accused. The accused admitted to having sexual intercourse with the girl and intending to marry her. Witnesses testified that the accused induced the girl to accompany him to a designated place. The girl was later found with the accused at a farm near Modasa. The prosecution alleged that the accused had enticed the girl to leave her parents' custody with the intention of marriage and to engage in sexual intercourse.
physical_harm: Sexual intercourse and pressure to marry
premeditation_planning: No pre-planning or use of weapon
motive: Love affair and intention to marry
key_evidence_accepted: The testimonies of numerous witnesses made out a clear case of enticement, and the evidence on record further unequivocally suggested that the appellant induced the prosecutrix to reach at a designated place to accompany him.
witness_credibility: The testimonies of witnesses made out a clear case of enticement, and the evidence on record further unequivocally suggested that the appellant induced the prosecutrix to reach at a designated place to accompany him.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 14.05.1998; Trial judgment: 16.12.2002; High Court decision: 28.07.2009; Supreme Court decision: 12.01.2021
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: Not stated; Counsel for the State: Not stated
investigation_status: FIR registered on 16.05.1998; charge sheet filed; trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction under Sections 363, 366 and 376 of IPC; High Court: Upheld conviction under Sections 363 and 366 of IPC; Supreme Court: Partly allowed the appeal, reduced sentence to period of incarceration already undergone
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellant enticed and took the minor girl, aged 16, from her lawful guardianship, with the intention to marry her and engage in sexual intercourse, thereby satisfying the elements of kidnapping under Sections 361 and 366 of the IPC.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the appellant and the prosecutrix were in a consensual relationship, and the prosecutrix voluntarily joined his company, thus negating the elements of kidnapping and the need for a criminal conviction.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that the act of enticing or taking a minor, along with the establishment of minority and lawful guardianship, is essential for the offence of kidnapping. Consent of a minor is immaterial under Section 361 of the IPC.
precedent_relied_upon: King Emperor v. Gokaran AIR 1921 Oudh 226; Emperor v. Abdur Rahman AIR 1916 All 210; S. Varadarajan v. State of Madras [1965] 1 SCR 243; State of Madhya Pradesh v. Surendra Singh (2015) 1 SCC 222; State of Haryana v. Raja Ram (1973) 1 SCC 544; Thakorlal D. Vadgama vs. State of Gujarat (1973) 2 SCC 413
sentencing_rationale: The sentence was reduced to the period already served due to the mildness of the crime, the appellant's young age at the time of the incident, the prolonged trial, and the appellant's rehabilitation and lack of recidivism.
judicial_mitigating_factors: The appellant's young age at the time of the incident, the prolonged trial, his rehabilitation, and the fact that the crime was one of passion with no recidivism.
other_sentence_order: The appellant's sentence was reduced to the period of incarceration already undergone by him.
neutral_facts_raw: The accused, a young man, was involved in an incident where a minor girl, aged 16, was taken from her parents' custody. The girl was working as a maid and was last seen leaving her workplace with the accused. The accused admitted to having sexual intercourse with the girl and intending to marry her. Witnesses testified that the accused induced the girl to accompany him to a designated place. The girl was later found with the accused at a farm near Modasa. The prosecution alleged that the accused had enticed the girl to leave her parents' custody with the intention of marriage and to engage in sexual intercourse. The trial court convicted the accused under sections 363 and 366 of the IPC, while the High Court upheld the conviction but reduced the sentence. The Supreme Court reviewed the case, considering the accused's young age, the nature of the relationship, and the lack of force or pre-planning, and ultimately reduced the sentence to the period already served.

title: HEM RAJ S/O. MOTI RAM versus STATE OF HARYANA
case_title: Hem Raj S/o. Moti Ram v. State of Haryana
trial_court_outcome: Convicted and sentenced to 7 years RI and 2 years RI
neutral_facts: The accused, a male, was alleged to have raped the victim, a female, during the night. The victim was 19 years old at the time of the incident. The prosecution relied on the victim's testimony, which was inconsistent and retracted. The victim's brother provided evidence, but it was found to be unreliable. The prosecution failed to examine the doctor who had examined the victim, and the medical report indicated that the victim's hymen was torn. However, the court found the victim's evidence to be unreliable and the brother's testimony insufficient to corroborate the claim. The prosecution also failed to present conclusive medical evidence linking the accused to the rape.
physical_harm: Injuries or death not specifically mentioned
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court did not accept the prosecution's case as it found the prosecutrix's evidence unreliable and insufficient, and the evidence of her brother and the medical report inconclusive.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the prosecutrix's credibility as extremely low, declaring her hostile due to her inconsistent statements and lack of cooperation. The brother's evidence was also found to be unsatisfactory and contradictory.
trial_duration: Offence: 12.30 A.M. on 12/3/1991; Trial judgment: 3/8/2001; High Court decision: 22.11.2011; Supreme Court decision: January 3, 2014
legal_representation: For the accused: D.P. Singh, Sonam Gupta, Salil Bhattacharya, Rajkiran Vais, Ravi Prakash Vyas (for Shivaji M. Jadhav); For the State: Deepkaran Dalal, AAG, Naresh Bakshi
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
procedural_irregularity: Failure of prosecution to examine the doctor who had examined the prosecutrix
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction and sentence; High Court: Dismissed the appeal; Supreme Court: Appeal allowed, conviction and sentences set aside
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the evidence of the prosecutrix, along with the Medico Legal Report (MLR), establishes the case of rape. They contended that the MLR supports the prosecution's case and that the appellant's conviction should be upheld.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the prosecutrix's evidence is unreliable and contradictory, and that her statement to the police was not acknowledged by her. They also pointed out that the evidence of her brother is inconsistent and lacks corroboration, and that the prosecution failed to examine the doctor who had examined the prosecutrix.
legal_principle_applied: The court emphasized that the evidence of the prosecutrix is most vital in a rape case and must be scrutinized carefully. If found credible, it can be relied upon even without corroboration, but the court may look into other evidence if hesitant to place implicit reliance on it.
precedent_relied_upon: State of Maharashtra v. Chandraprakash Kewalchand Jain [1990] 1 SCR 115
sentencing_rationale: Not applicable
other_sentence_order: The court quashed and set aside the conviction and sentence of the appellant under Sections 376 and 450 of the IPC and directed the appellant to be released forthwith, unless required in any other case.
neutral_facts_raw: The accused, a male, was alleged to have raped the victim, a female, during the night. The victim was 19 years old at the time of the incident. The prosecution relied on the victim's testimony, which was inconsistent and retracted. The victim's brother provided evidence, but it was found to be unreliable. The prosecution failed to examine the doctor who had examined the victim, and the medical report indicated that the victim's hymen was torn. However, the court found the victim's evidence to be unreliable and the brother's testimony insufficient to corroborate the claim. The prosecution also failed to present conclusive medical evidence linking the accused to the rape. The court ultimately found the prosecution's case unsustainable and acquitted the accused.

title: NARESH KUMAR versus STATE OF HARYANA
case_title: Naresh Kumar v. State of Haryana
trial_court_outcome: Convicted
neutral_facts: The accused, Naresh Kumar, was married to the deceased, Rani, who committed suicide by consuming poison on 19 November 1993. The prosecution alleged that the accused's repeated demands for money to start a business contributed to her suicide. The deceased's brother and father testified that the accused had demanded money from the deceased and her parents, causing her to remain tense. However, the evidence did not establish any form of incessant cruelty or harassment on the part of the accused that would have compelled the deceased to commit suicide. The deceased's family stated that the accused had left for Delhi after the shop was wound up, and the deceased had remained tense due to the financial demands.
offence_severity: Imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine
physical_harm: No injuries or death caused, except the deceased committed suicide
number_of_offences: The appellant was charged with one offence under Section 306 IPC, but the High Court upheld the conviction, which was later set aside by the Supreme Court
premeditation_planning: The court found no premeditation or planning, as the prosecution failed to establish the required mens rea and active act
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted that the prosecution failed to establish the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt, as there was no cogent evidence of harassment or cruelty leading to the deceased's suicide.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses (PW-4 and PW-5) as stating that there was a demand for money by the accused, but their evidence did not disclose any form of incessant cruelty or harassment which would drag the wife to commit suicide.
bail_history: Pending the present appeal, vide order dated 13.05.2009 a coordinate Bench had ordered release of the convict on bail. Since the appeal is being allowed and the convict is being acquitted, the bail bond(s) furnished then shall also stand discharged
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 19-11-1993; Trial judgment: 08.09.1998/10.09.1998; High Court decision: 03.09.2008; Supreme Court decision: 22 February 2024
legal_representation: S.D. Singh, Mrs. Shweta Sinha, Ram Kripal Singh, Siddharth Singh, Mrs. Aparna Jha, Advs. for the Appellant; Raj Singh Rana, A.A.G., Samar Vijay Singh, Keshav Mittal, Ms. Sabarni Som, Fateh Singh, Advs. for the Respondent
investigation_status: Charge sheet filed; trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction affirmed; High Court: Conviction affirmed; Supreme Court: Appeal allowed, conviction set aside, appellant acquitted
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the deceased committed suicide due to incessant harassment by the appellant, and that the courts below correctly applied the presumption under Section 113A of the Evidence Act to convict the appellant under Section 306 of the IPC.
defence_argument: The defence argued that there was no cogent evidence of harassment or cruelty by the appellant, and that the conviction was not sustainable as the prosecution failed to establish the required mens rea and active act leading to the deceased's suicide.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that for a conviction under Section 306 IPC, there must be a clear mens rea, an active act or direct act leading to the deceased's suicide, and that the presumption under Section 113A of the Evidence Act is discretionary and requires proof of cruelty or incessant harassment.
precedent_relied_upon: Geo Varghese v. State of Rajasthan and another, [2021] 10 SCR 393 : (2021) 19 SCC 144; M. Arjunan v. State, represented by its Inspector of Police, (2019) 3 SCC 315; Ude Singh & Others v. State of Haryana, [2019] 9 SCR 703 : (2019) 17 SCC 301; Mariano Anto Bruno & another v. The Inspector of Police, [2022] 14 SCR 889 : (2022) SCC Online SC 1387; Gurcharan Singh v. State of Punjab, [2020] 8 SCR 741 : (2020) 10 SCC 200; Kashibai & Others v. The State of Karnataka, [2023] 3 SCR 175 : (2023) SCC Online SC 575; Lakhjit Singh v. State of Punjab, (1994) Suppl. 1 SCC 173; Pawan Kumar v. State of Haryana, [1998] 1 SCR 746 : (1998) (3) SCC 309; Smt. Shanti v. State of Haryana, [1990] Suppl. 2 SCR 675 : (1991) 1 SCC 371
sentencing_rationale: Not applicable
neutral_facts_raw: The accused, Naresh Kumar, was married to the deceased, Rani, who committed suicide by consuming poison on 19 November 1993. The prosecution alleged that the accused's repeated demands for money to start a business contributed to her suicide. The deceased's brother and father testified that the accused had demanded money from the deceased and her parents, causing her to remain tense. However, the evidence did not establish any form of incessant cruelty or harassment on the part of the accused that would have compelled the deceased to commit suicide. The deceased's family stated that the accused had left for Delhi after the shop was wound up, and the deceased had remained tense due to the financial demands. The trial court and High Court convicted the accused under Section 306 of the IPC, but the Supreme Court overturned the conviction, finding that the prosecution failed to prove the necessary mens rea and active act required for abetment of suicide.

title: STATE OF PUNJAB versus KEWAL KRISHAN

title: RAMSWAROOP AND ANOTHER versus STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH

title: TAIJUDDIN versus STATE OF ASSAM & ORS.

The accused was arrested and a case was registered against him under Section 379 of the Indian Penal Code. key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the circumstantial evidence, including the recovery of the dead body of the deceased based on the alleged confessional statement of the appellant, but found it insufficient to establish guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the credibility of the witnesses, noting that there was no specific identification mark on the recovered sheep to link them to the deceased, and that the recovery of the dead body was based on a confessional statement which was denied by the appellant.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 27.01.2000; Trial judgment: 3rd July, 2015; High Court decision: 27.02.2006; Supreme Court decision: 11.10.2018

defence_argument: The accused contended that the requirements of Section 195(1)(b)(i) and Section 340, Cr.P.C. were not complied with prior to framing the charge under Section 193, IPC, and that the investigation stage did not constitute a proceeding in any court for the purpose of Section 195(1)(b)(i), Cr.P.C.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that the words 'in relation to' under Section 195(1)(b)(i), Cr.P.C. must be interpreted with a reasonably close nexus to the court proceedings, and that the investigation stage, while a stage of a judicial proceeding, does not equate to a proceeding in any court under Section 195(1)(b)(i), Cr.P.C.
precedent_relied_upon: Sachida Nand Singh and Another v. State of Bihar and Another, (1998) 2 SCC 493; Patel Laljibhai Somabhai AIR 1971 SC 1935; Iqbal Singh Marwah and Another v. Meenakshi Marwah and Another, (2005) 4 SCC 370
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed due to the gravity of the offence, the elaborate conspiracy to fabricate false evidence, and the attempt to shield the appellant from prosecution, despite the High Court's leniency in reducing the sentences.
judicial_mitigating_factors: The High Court considered the advanced age of the accused and the delay in completion of the trial as mitigating factors.
other_sentence_order: The Appellants are directed to surrender for serving out the rest of their sentence, and the Registry is directed to release any fine deposited before the Court.
neutral_facts_raw: The accused, including a regional manager, were involved in a scheme to fabricate false evidence to shield one accused from prosecution in a case involving disproportionate assets. However, the investigation revealed that the market value of the properties was much lower than the claimed amount, and the stamp papers used were illegal. The accused were found to have conspired to create a false sale agreement to mislead the investigation. The trial court convicted the accused for fabricating false evidence, and the high court confirmed this finding.

defence_argument: The defence argued that the act was done in a sudden fight and without premeditation, and that the burning was accidental due to the victim wearing a nylon sari, not an intentional act to cause death.

neutral_facts_raw: The accused came home under the influence of liquor and started abusing his wife. The victim was wearing a nylon sari, which caught fire and caused her to be engulfed in flames. She was taken to the hospital, where she was found to have sustained burns covering 70% of her body. In her dying declaration, she stated that the accused had tried to douse the fire. The accused also sustained burn injuries covering 18% of his body. The prosecution relied on the dying declaration to establish the accused's intent to cause death or grievous harm, leading to a conviction under Section 302 IPC. post_offence_conduct: The appellant was declared a proclaimed offender and was directed to surrender before the Trial Court, but he appeared and was granted interim bail. The court found no justification to continue proceedings against him after the dispute was resolved.
bail_history: Bail granted by the High Court subject to conditions, interim bail granted by the Trial Court
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 29.10.2009; Trial judgment: 26.09.2014; High Court decision: 10.01.2020; Supreme Court decision: 24.09.2021
legal_representation: Lakhwinder Singh Mann, Dr. Surender Singh Hooda for the Appellant; Ms. Jaspreet Gogia, Ms. Mandakini Singh, Karanvir Gogia, Ms. Shivangi Singhal, Ms. Ashima Mandla for the Respondents
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Proceedings against Gurmeet Singh compounded; High Court: Declined to quash proceedings; Supreme Court: Quashed proceedings against the appellant
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the FIR was valid and that the appellant's name was specifically mentioned in the FIR, thus justifying the continuation of criminal proceedings against him.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the dispute was civil in nature, the complainant had already settled his score with the main accused, and the proceedings against the appellant were unjustified and amounted to abuse of process.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that the inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC should be exercised to prevent abuse of process of any court and to secure the ends of justice, particularly in cases with a predominantly civil flavour where the dispute has been resolved.

The complainant also alleged that the accused demanded additional money and threatened dire consequences if the money was not paid. The investigating officers initially found no substance in the complaint and recommended closure, but the senior superintendent of police directed the registration of an FIR. The police report concluded that a triable case was made out only against the main accused, while the other accused were exonerated. The complainant later entered into a compromise with the main accused, which was accepted by the court, leading to the closure of proceedings against the main accused. The other accused were summoned for trial, but the complainant had already settled his dispute with the main accused, and there was no justification to continue the proceedings against the other accused.

title: KHIM SINGH versus STATE OF UTTARAKHAND
case_title: Khim Singh v. State of Uttarakhand
aggravating_circumstances: Quarrels between accused and victim, failure to explain whereabouts, blood-stained weapon found at accused's house, door not bolted from inside
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under Section 302 IPC and sentenced to life imprisonment
neutral_facts: The accused, Khim Singh, and his wife, Himuli Devi, lived together in their house. They had frequent quarrels, with a specific incident occurring in the evening of July 17, 1987. On the morning of July 18, 1987, a neighbor discovered Himuli Devi dead inside their house. The house was locked from the inside, and no one else was present. The victim had injuries consistent with a sharp-edged weapon, and a blood-stained weapon was later found at the accused's house. The accused failed to explain his whereabouts during the night of the incident, and the door of the house was not bolted from the inside. The prosecution relied on circumstantial evidence, including witness statements and the condition of the weapon, to establish the accused's involvement in the victim's death.
physical_harm: Injuries on the deceased's head, including an incised wound and contusion, leading to death due to shock and haemorrhage
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the circumstantial evidence, including the testimony of witnesses, the presence of the accused in the house, the unnatural conduct of the accused, the recovery of the blood-stained Kulhari, and the medical report indicating the cause of death.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as credible, particularly Manuli Devi (PW-1) and Bachi Singh (PW-4), noting their statements about the quarrels and the circumstances surrounding the death, and found their testimony to be reliable and corroborative.
post_offence_conduct: The conduct of the accused in the morning of 18th July, 1987 was unnatural; he failed to explain his whereabouts on the fateful night and did not contact the Pradhan or Patwari to lodge a report.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 17th-18th July 1987; Trial judgment: 30th March 1988; High Court decision: 24th August 2005; Supreme Court decision: 8th July 2014
legal_representation: Feroze Ahmad, R.S. Sharma for the Appellant; Mukesh Verma, Pankaj K. Singh, Jatinder Kumar Bhatia for the Respondent
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Convicted under Section 302 IPC and sentenced to life imprisonment; High Court: Affirmed the conviction and sentence; Supreme Court: Dismissed the appeal, upheld the conviction and sentence
prosecution_argument: The prosecution relied on circumstantial evidence, including witness testimonies about frequent quarrels between the appellant and his wife, the absence of others in the house on the night of the murder, the unnatural conduct of the appellant in the morning, and the recovery of a blood-stained Kulhari at the appellant's house.
defence_argument: The defence argued that there was no complete chain of circumstantial evidence to prove the appellant's guilt, and that the witnesses were hostile, leading to insufficient evidence to convict the appellant solely on suspicion without an eye-witness.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that a chain of circumstantial evidence can be sufficient to prove guilt if it forms a complete and logical sequence of events leading to the conclusion of the accused's involvement in the crime.
precedent_relied_upon: Not stated
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence of life imprisonment was imposed because the prosecution successfully proved the appellant's involvement in the murder through a complete chain of circumstantial evidence, and the High Court affirmed the conviction and sentence.
other_sentence_order: The Supreme Court directed payment of Rs.7,000/- as fee to the amicus curiae.

The victim had injuries consistent with a sharp-edged weapon, and a blood-stained weapon was later found at the accused's house. The accused failed to explain his whereabouts during the night of the incident, and the door of the house was not bolted from the inside. The prosecution relied on circumstantial evidence, including witness statements and the condition of the weapon, to establish the accused's involvement in the victim's death.

title: MOSIRUDDIN MUNSHI versus MD. SIRAJ AND ANOTHER
case_title: MOSIRUDDIN MUNSHI v. MD. SIRAJ AND ANOTHER
trial_court_outcome: Forwarded complaint for investigation
neutral_facts: The accused, through a public servant, represented that they could arrange for a plot of land for sale. The accused and the complainant entered into an agreement for sale, and the complainant paid a large sum of money in cash. The accused failed to hand over the title documents, leading the complainant to issue a legal notice. When other methods to compel the accused to complete the sale failed, the complainant filed a criminal complaint against the accused under Sections 420 and 1208 of the IPC. The accused then filed an application under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. to quash the proceedings.
offence_severity: Minimum 6 months to maximum 7 years of imprisonment
physical_harm: Not stated
key_evidence_accepted: The complaint makes averments so as to infer fraudulent or dishonest inducement having been made by respondent No.1 and accused No.2 pursuant to which the appellant parted with money.
witness_credibility: Not stated
trial_duration: Dates of offence: January 2005; Trial judgment: Not stated; High Court decision: June 29, 2010; Supreme Court decision: May 9, 2014
legal_representation: Sumanta Chakrabarty, Chandan Kumar Rai for the Appellant; Pijush K. Roy, Kakali Roy, Mithilesh Kumar Singh for the Respondents
investigation_status: Investigation was initiated by the Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate and forwarded to the officer in-charge of the Amherst Street Police Station for investigation
appeal_history: Trial court: Not stated; High Court: Quashed the complaint proceedings; Supreme Court: Appeal allowed, order setting aside the impugned order
prosecution_argument: The complaint made by the appellant-complainant contains averments that would prima facie make out a case for investigation, as it infers fraudulent or dishonest inducement by the respondents and accused, leading to the appellant parting with money.
defence_argument: The dispute involved in the complaint is of a civil nature, and none of the acts allegedly committed by the respondent gave rise to any criminal liability, as rightly held by the High Court.
legal_principle_applied: The High Court should not quash a criminal proceeding unless the allegations in the FIR, even if taken at face value, do not disclose commission of a cognizable offence. The Court should not go beyond the allegations in the FIR and should allow investigation to proceed if there is a prima facie case.
precedent_relied_upon: Hridaya Ranjan Prasad Verma and others vs. State of Bihar and another (2000) 4 SCC 168; Murari Lal Gupta vs. Gopi Singh (2005) 13 SCC 699; Ram Biraji Devi and another vs. Umesh Kumar Singh and another (2006) 6 SCC 669; R. Kalyani vs. Janak C. Mehta (2009) 1 SCC 516; Mahesh Chaudhary vs. State of Rajasthan (2009) 4 SCC 443
sentencing_rationale: Not applicable
neutral_facts_raw: The accused, through a public servant, represented that they could arrange for a plot of land for sale. The accused and the complainant entered into an agreement for sale, and the complainant paid a large sum of money in cash. The accused failed to hand over the title documents, leading the complainant to issue a legal notice. When other methods to compel the accused to complete the sale failed, the complainant filed a criminal complaint against the accused under Sections 420 and 1208 of the IPC. The trial court forwarded the complaint for investigation, treating it as a First Information Report. The accused then filed an application under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. to quash the proceedings. The High Court quashed the complaint proceedings, declaring it a civil transaction. The case was remitted to the High Court for a fresh decision, which again quashed the proceedings. The complainant appealed to the Supreme Court, which allowed the appeal and set aside the High Court's order.
